metadata.title: Adolescent Loneliness Trends and Contextual Correlates Across 38 Countries From 2000 to 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA microdata for 15- and 16-year-old students across 38 OECD-member countries and multiple survey years (2000, 2003, 2012, 2015, 2018, 2022). PISA’s two-stage stratified sampling (schools selected with PPS to enrollment of 15-year-olds, then students sampled within schools) is used to obtain nationally representative data, and the authors apply weights to account for differences in country population size. Specifically, they construct standardized country weights by summing PISA-provided student weights within each country and year, then scaling each country’s contribution by the relative average population represented across the 38 countries. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the analysis is not framed as ML prediction; instead it uses weighted multilevel regression models with covariates and piecewise time trends.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a constructed loneliness scale mean from PISA questionnaire items (Likert responses), not a cognitive achievement score with PISA plausible values. Because the analysis is based on questionnaire responses and the paper only reports exclusion for students who skipped any loneliness questions, it does not describe a broader missing-data imputation strategy for other variables. This is therefore a reporting gap for missingness handling beyond the stated loneliness-item exclusion rule.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Included students aged 15 and 16 who completed the OECD PISA survey and were administered the sense of belonging questionnaire in 2000, 2003, 2012, 2015, 2018, or 2022. For loneliness measurement, the study restricted to students within OECD-member countries who had the loneliness items available for the relevant year; in 2022, students were randomly assigned 5 of the 6 loneliness questions. Excluded students who skipped any loneliness questions (N=52,068), yielding a final population of 1,267,476 students. For country-level correlates, COVID-19-related variables were restricted to 2022 only; internet-use analyses were restricted to 2012–2018 because the internet questions were unavailable before 2012 and changed in 2022.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000-2022 (15- and 16-year-olds), loneliness scale (sense of belonging questionnaire)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Piecewise multilevel regression (weighted): 2000–2012 adjusted beta = -0.007 (95% CI: -0.022, 0.008); 2012–2015 adjusted beta = 0.045 (95% CI: 0.035, 0.054); 2015–2022 adjusted beta = 0.017 (95% CI: 0.008, 0.025). Model includes 1,169,308 individuals clustered within 38 countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000-2022 the study leveraged sex, maternal education, and paternal education to estimate piecewise multilevel trends in school loneliness, finding that loneliness slightly decreased from 2000 to 2012 but increased substantially from 2012 to 2015 and continued to rise (though less) from 2015 to 2022. This indicates that adolescent loneliness has worsened during the early-2010s period and remained elevated thereafter, supporting policy attention to sustained social-connection interventions rather than short-term responses.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (15- and 16-year-olds), loneliness scale (sense of belonging questionnaire)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-level COVID-19 correlates (grand-mean centered; adjusted for sex, maternal education, paternal education): COVID-19 cumulative mortality adjusted beta = 0.002 (95% CI: -0.001, 0.006); Oxford Stringency Index adjusted beta = -0.001 (95% CI: -0.007, 0.005). Sample: n=235,779; c=35 countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 the study leveraged COVID-19 cumulative mortality and public health stringency (with adjustment for sex, maternal education, and paternal education) to predict school loneliness, finding effects close to zero and not statistically significant. This indicates that, within OECD countries and by 2022, cross-national differences in COVID-19 mortality and policy stringency did not measurably translate into loneliness differences, suggesting other social mechanisms beyond pandemic severity may be more relevant.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes OECD PISA loneliness data for 15- and 16-year-olds across 38 countries and survey years 2000, 2003, 2012, 2015, 2018, and 2022 (final analytic population: 1,267,476 after excluding students who skipped any loneliness items). Loneliness is measured as a weighted mean of 6 (or 5 in 2022) sense-of-belonging items on a 4-point Likert scale. The authors use weighted multilevel piecewise regression to estimate time trends and Fairbrother-style decomposition to separate between-country and within-country associations. Adjusted loneliness trends show a non-significant slight decrease from 2000–2012 (beta=-0.007) followed by a significant increase from 2012–2015 (beta=0.045) and a smaller increase from 2015–2022 (beta=0.017). For correlates, COVID-19 mortality and stringency in 2022 are near zero and non-significant, while within-country increases in internet use (2012–2018) and unemployment (2000–2022) are associated with lower loneliness. Limitations include reliance on observational associations (no causality) and no explicit missing-data strategy beyond loneliness-item exclusion.
